title: Recognise, group, use and care for materials which can impact on health and the environment

lessons.title: Materials that can harm health and the environment
lessons.html:
Materials around us

On a farm we use many materials every day. Most are safe. Some can hurt people, animals, soil and water if we use them wrongly. We call these hazardous materials.

Grouping materials

GroupFarm examplesPossible harm
PoisonsRat poison, dips, sprays for ticks and fliesPoisoning people, horses, dogs, birds
Fuels and oilsDiesel, petrol, engine oil, paraffinFire, burns, polluting soil and water
CorrosivesBattery acid, strong cleaners, caustic sodaBurns to skin and eyes
Gases and fumesGas bottles, exhaust smoke, welding fumesBreathing problems, explosions
DustsDusty hay, cement, fertiliser dustCoughing, lung problems in people and horses
Plastics and metalsFeed bags, twine, wire, tinsInjure animals, litter, do not rot

Read the label

Every chemical has a label. The label tells you what it is, how to use it, what protective clothing to wear and what to do if there is an accident. If you cannot read the label well, ask your supervisor to explain it. Never use a product from an unmarked bottle.

Warning pictures

Labels have pictures in a red diamond. Learn them:

  • Skull and crossbones - poison, can kill
  • Flame - catches fire easily
  • Hand and metal being eaten away - burns skin
  • Dead fish and tree - harms the environment and water
  • Exclamation mark - harmful, irritates

How harm gets into the body

Chemicals can get in by breathing them, swallowing them, through the skin, or into the eyes. This is why we wear gloves, masks and goggles, and why we never eat or smoke while working with chemicals.

lessons.title: Using, storing and caring for hazardous materials
lessons.html:
Using materials safely

  1. Read the label or ask your supervisor before you start.
  2. Wear the protective clothing the label asks for: gloves, overall, boots, mask, goggles.
  3. Use only the amount you need. More is not better.
  4. Mix chemicals outside or in a place with fresh air, away from water troughs and feed.
  5. Keep people, children and animals away while you work.
  6. Never eat, drink or smoke while working.
  7. Wash your hands and face when you finish.

Storing materials

  • Keep chemicals in their own labelled containers. Never put them in cooldrink bottles.
  • Lock poisons in the chemical store, away from the feed room.
  • Store fuel away from the stables and away from fire. Keep a fire extinguisher near.
  • Keep gas bottles upright and in the shade.
  • Store hay dry and off the ground so it does not go mouldy.

Spills

If a chemical or diesel spills:

  1. Keep people and horses away.
  2. Tell your supervisor.
  3. Stop the spill if it is safe, for example stand the drum upright.
  4. Cover it with sand or soil to soak it up. Do not hose it into a drain or river.
  5. Put the dirty sand in a marked container for safe disposal.

If someone is poisoned or splashed

Get the person away from the chemical. Wash skin or eyes with lots of clean water. Take the label or container with you to the clinic so the nurse knows what it was. Call for help at once. Proper first aid needs hands-on training from an accredited provider.

Caring for the environment

Do not let chemicals, oil or dirty water run into rivers, dams or boreholes. Pick up wire, plastic and twine from the camps. Reuse or recycle what you can. Every worker helps keep the farm safe for the next generation.

Key points

  • Group materials: poisons, fuels, corrosives, gases, dusts, plastics and metals.
  • Always read the label and learn the warning pictures.
  • Wear protective clothing and never eat or smoke while using chemicals.
  • Store chemicals locked, labelled and away from feed.
  • Soak up spills with sand; never wash them into water.
